{{short description|none}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=July 2021}}
[[File:Stadio Olimpico Torino Italy.jpg|thumb|200px|Stadio Olimpico di Torino (Turin Olympic Stadium) as a football venue in 2008. For the 2006 Winter Olympics, it hosted the opening and closing ceremonies.]]
For the [[2006 Winter Olympics]] in [[Turin]], [[Italy]], a total of fifteen '''sports venues''' were used. Venue construction ran from 2002 to 2005. Cesana Pariol had to have turns 17 and 18 modified following the Luge World Cup in January 2005, but they were not cleared out until October 2005. Winds postponed the Nordic combined team event for a day. Many of the venues served as host for the Winter Universidade the following year.

{{2006 Winter Olympics}}

==Before the Olympics==
[[File:Palavela-Interno.jpg|thumb|200px|Palavela during the 2006 Winter Olympics. The venue hosted the figure skating and short track speed skating events during those games.]]
Stadio Olimpico in 1934 was known as Stadio [[Benito Mussolini]]. For the [[FIFA World Cup]] that took place [[1934 FIFA World Cup|that year]], the stadium hosted two matches, including the quarterfinal match between [[Czechoslovakia]] and [[Switzerland]].<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20070921085535/http://fifa.com/worldcup/archive/edition=3/results/matches/match=1104/report.html FIFA.com World Cup Turin Benito Mussolini 27 May 1934 AUT-FRA results.]. Retrieved 27 December 2010.</ref><ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20070921085416/http://fifa.com/worldcup/archive/edition=3/results/matches/match=1143/report.html FIFA.com World Cup Turin Benito Mussolini 31 May 1934 TCH-SUI quarterfinal results.]. Retrieved 27 December 2010.</ref>

Turin was selected by the [[Italian Olympic Committee]] to be selected to host the 2006 Winter Olympics in March 1998. It was awarded the 2006 Winter Olympics on 19 June 1999.<ref>[http://www.la84foundation.org/6oic/OfficialReports/2006/2006v3.pdf 2006 Winter Olympics official report.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120907001546/http://www.la84foundation.org/6oic/OfficialReports/2006/2006v3.pdf |date=7 September 2012 }} Volume 3. p. 17. Retrieved 27 December 2010. {{in lang|en|it}}</ref>

Cesana Pariol construction began in 2002 and was completed in 2004. After a Luge World Cup test event in January 2005 that was abandoned to accidents. This led to modifications of Turns 17 and 18 and a retest of the track that was approved by the [[International Luge Federation]] (FIL) in October 2005.<ref name=cp /> Oval Lingotto opened on 9 December 2005.<ref name=ol /> Palavela, constructed in 1961, was modified for the 2006 Games to host figure skating and short track speed skating events.<ref name=pv /> San Sicario Fraiteve hosted an [[Alpine Skiing World Cup]] in February 2005, and was modified to make the women's super-G event more challenging.<ref name=ssf /> Torino Esposizinoi was constructed in 1949 and refurbished in time for the 2006 Games to host the preliminary ice hockey matches.<ref name=te />

Venues were selected between May 2001 and the summer of 2002. Construction of the venues ran between the summers of 2002 and 2005. The venues were turned over for use of the 2006 Games between the summer of 2005 and February 2006.<ref>[http://www.la84foundation.org/6oic/OfficialReports/2006/2006v3.pdf 2006 Winter Olympics official report.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120907001546/http://www.la84foundation.org/6oic/OfficialReports/2006/2006v3.pdf |date=7 September 2012 }} Volume 3. pp. 114-5. Retrieved 27 December 2010. {{in lang|en|it}}</ref> New construction included Cesana Pariol, Cesana San Sicario, Pragelato, Pragelato Plan, and Sauze d'Ouix-Jouvencaux while the other venues used were refurbished or expanded.<ref>[http://www.la84foundation.org/6oic/OfficialReports/2006/2006v2.pdf 2006 Winter Olympics official report.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110114082242/http://www.la84foundation.org/6oic/OfficialReports/2006/2006v2.pdf |date=14 January 2011 }} Volume 2. pp. 66-8. Retrieved 28 December 2010. {{in lang|en|it}}</ref> Sustainability efforts were applied on all venues, but the most noted in the Olympics report were Cesana Pariol and Pragelato Plan.<ref>[http://www.la84foundation.org/6oic/OfficialReports/2006/2006v2.pdf 2006 Winter Olympics official report.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110114082242/http://www.la84foundation.org/6oic/OfficialReports/2006/2006v2.pdf |date=14 January 2011 }} Volume 2. pp. 104-5. Retrieved 28 December 2010. {{in lang|en|it}}</ref> The most expensive venue construction in the Mountain area was Cesana Pariol at [[Euro|€]]85.78 million while the most expensive city venue used for competition in the City area was Oval Lingotto at €74.27 million.<ref>[http://www.la84foundation.org/6oic/OfficialReports/2006/2006v2.pdf 2006 Winter Olympics official report.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110114082242/http://www.la84foundation.org/6oic/OfficialReports/2006/2006v2.pdf |date=14 January 2011 }} Volume 2. pp. 182-3. Retrieved 28 December 2010. {{in lang|en|it}}</ref>

==During the Olympics==
[[File:Cesana Torinese-Bobsleigh.jpg|thumb|200px|Picture of turns 15 through 19 (right to left) of Cesana Pariol during the 2006 Winter Olympics. Bobsleigh, luge, and skeleton events took place at this venue.]]
The men's curling bronze medal match at Pinerolo between [[Great Britain at the 2006 Winter Olympics|Great Britain]] and the [[United States at the 2006 Winter Olympics|United States]] was interrupted by a [[streaking|streaker]] wearing a [[rubber chicken]] as a [[loin cloth]].<ref>Wallechinsky, David and Jaime Loucky (2009). " Curling: Men". In ''The complete Book of the Winter Olympics: 2010 Edition''. London: Aurum Press Limited. pp. 151-2.</ref>

At Cesana Pariol, the [[Luge at the 2006 Winter Olympics – Women's singles|women's singles luge]] event had thirteen crashes or near crashes during the four runs. Among those who crashed were American [[Samantha Retrosi]] who was knocked unconscious at the end of the second run while [[Italy at the 2006 Winter Olympics|Italy]]'s [[Anastasia Oberstolz-Antonova]] crashed out during the first run.<ref>Wallechinsky, David and Jaime Loucky (2009). "Luge (Toboggan): Women". In ''The Complete Book of the Winter Olympics: 2010 Edition''. London: Aurum Press Limited. p. 173.</ref>

During the [[Alpine skiing at the 2006 Winter Olympics – Men's super-G|men's super-G alpine skiing]] event at Sestriere Borgata, seventeen skiers had gone down the course in the morning portion of the event before it was halted to heavy snowfall. The event was restarted in the afternoon with all morning results cancelled. [[Norway at the 2006 Winter Olympics|Norway]]'s [[Kjetil André Aamodt]] won the event.<ref>Wallechinsky, David and Jaime Loucky (2009). "Alpine Skiing, Men: Super Giant Slalom". In ''The Complete Book of the Winter Olympics: 2010 Edition''. London: Aurum Press Limited. p. 193.</ref>

San Sicario Fraiteve had its [[Alpine skiing at the 2006 Winter Olympics – Women's downhill|women's downhill alpine skiing]] course modified at the request of [[Austria at the 2006 Winter Olympics|Austria]]'s [[Michaela Dorfmeister]] who complained that the course was too easy. Modifications included bigger jumps and steeper banks and it was after a women's super-G event that was a test event in 2005.<ref>Wallechinsky, David and Jaime Loucky (2009). "Alpine Skiing, Women: Downhill". In ''The Complete Book of the Winter Olympics: 2010 Edition''. London: Aurum Press Limited. p. 212.</ref>

During the ski jumping portion of the [[Nordic combined at the 2006 Winter Olympics – Team|Nordic combined team]] event, it was postponed halfway through to strong winds. They resumed the next day with [[Germany at the 2006 Winter Olympics|Germany]] having a 10-second lead over Austria going into the cross-country portion of the event. At the halfway point of the final leg, Austria's [[Mario Stecher]] overcame a 20-second deficit to defeat Germany's [[Jens Gaiser]] by 15.3 seconds.<ref>Wallechinsky, David and Jaime Loucky (2009). "Nordic Combined: Team". In ''The Complete Book of the Winter Olympics: 2010 Edition''. London: Aurum Press Limited. p. 280.</ref>

==After the Olympics==
[[File:Pragelato olympic skijump.jpg|thumb|200px|Pragelato ski jump during the 2006 Winter Olympics. The venue hosted the ski jumping and the ski jumping portion of the Nordic combined events.]]
Oval Lingotto hosted the [[World Fencing Championships]] in [[2006 World Fencing Championships|2006]].<ref>[http://www.fie.ch/Competitions/Calendar.aspx?results=true FIE.ch listing of the 2006 World Fencing Championships in Turin.]. Retrieved 28 December 2010.</ref> Several of the venues used for the 2006 Games were also used for the Winter [[Universiade]] [[2007 Winter Universiade|the following year]]. They included Bardonecchia, Pragelato, Cesana San Sicario, Palavela, Pinerolo, and Oval Lingotto.<ref>[http://www.fisu.net/en/Torino-2007-Programme-1359.html FISU.net schedule of the 2007 Winter Universiade at Turin.]. Retrieved 28 December 2010.</ref> San Sicario Friateve's last World Cup event in alpine skiing was in 2007.<ref>[http://www.fis-ski.com/uk/604/1228.html?event_id=21936&cal_suchsector=AL FIS-ski.com Alpine Skiing World Cup San Sicario 26-28 January 2007 results.]. Retrieved 29 December 2010.</ref> Pragelato's last World Cup ski jumping event was in 2008.<ref>[http://www.fis-ski.com/uk/604/1228.html?event_id=24647&cal_suchsector=JP FIS-Ski.com Ski Jumping World Cup Pragelato 12-14 December 2008 results.]. Retrieved 29 December 2010.</ref> Bardonecchia's last snowboarding World Cup event was in 2009.<ref>[http://www.fis-ski.com/uk/604/1228.html?event_id=24729&cal_suchsector=SB FIS-ski.com Snowboarding World Cup Bardonecchia 5-7 February 2009 results.]. Retrieved 29 December 2010.</ref> Palavela hosted the [[World Figure Skating Championships]] in [[2010 World Figure Skating Championships|2010]].<ref>{{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20090924030211/http://www.torino2010.org/index.aspx Torino2010.org ISU 2010 World Figure Skating Championships official website.]}}. Retrieved 28 December 2010. {{in lang|en|it}}</ref> Cesana Pariol hosted the [[FIL European Luge Championships]] in [[FIL European Luge Championships 2008|2008]] and the [[FIL World Luge Championships]] [[FIL World Luge Championships 2011|three years later]].<ref>[http://www.fil-luge.org/fileadmin/user_upload/Documents/Statistik/EM/Namentliche_Ergebnisse_EM-KB.pdf FIL-Luge.org European Championships medalists: 1914-2010.]. Retrieved 29 December 2010.</ref><ref>[http://www.fil-luge.org/fileadmin/user_upload/Documents/Kalender/2010-2011/2010-2011_Sportkalender_KB.pdf FIL-Luge.org artificial track calendar: 2010-11.]. Retrieved 29 December 2010.</ref>
